title: Cap. 1 prol. IV: distinguishing conditions defined — free-will use
latin: Jam de conditionibus distinguentibus pauca etiam dicenda sunt. IV. Conditiones distinguentes appello, contrarios actus aut qualitates, quibus in subjecto praevisis & praeconsideratis, contrarii actus etiam in Deo circa idem subjectum exercentur. Verbi causa, bonus usus liberi arbitrii, & malus usus liberi arbitrii sunt actus contrarii: Si quis ergo sentiat ex praevisione boni usus secundum Dei ordinationem homines semper praedestinari, ex praevisione mali usus reprobari, is facit bonum & malum usum liberi arbitrii conditiones distinguentes in subjecto praedestinationis aut reprobationis requisitas.
pass_a: Now concerning distinguishing conditions a few things also are to be said. IV. I call distinguishing conditions contrary acts or qualities which, when foresight and preconsidered in the subject, contrary acts also are exercised in God concerning the same subject. For example, the good use of free choice and the bad use of free choice are contrary acts: If therefore anyone should hold that from the foresight of the good use, according to God's ordination, humans are always predestined, and from the foresight of the bad use are reprobated, that person makes the good and bad use of free choice into distinguishing conditions required in the subject of predestination or reprobation. Key lemmas: conditiones distinguentes (distinguishing conditions); praevisio (foresight); liberum arbitrium (free choice); praedestinari / reprobari.
pass_b: A few words now on distinguishing conditions. IV. By distinguishing conditions I mean contrary acts or qualities which, when foresight and weighed beforehand in the subject, bring about contrary acts in God toward that same subject. Take free choice: its good use and its bad use are contrary acts. If someone holds that, by God's ordination, foresight of the good use always means predestination, and foresight of the bad use means reprobation, then that person makes the good and bad use of free choice into distinguishing conditions required in the subject of predestination or reprobation.

title: Cap. 1 prol. IV: works foresight and faith foresight as distinguishers
latin: Sic etiam, si quis tueatur illos solos eligi ad gloriam, quos Deus praevidet meritis sive bonis operibus ornatos usque ad finem vitae suae, atque eos solos reprobari sive non-eligi, quos praevidet demeritis sive malis operibus perseveranter adhaerescentes, is praevisa opera, prout bona fuerint vel mala, ponit conditiones distinguentes, pro quarum differentia differentes actus Divinae praedestinationis & reprobationis diversis hominibus conveniunt. Item, si quis doceat Deum illos solos eligere quos praevidet perseveraturos in fide, illos solos praeterire & rejicere quos praevidet perseveraturos in infidelitate, is hanc fidem & infidelitatem constituit conditiones distinguentes, pro quarum discrimine distincti actus praedestinationis & reprobationis cadunt in distinctas personas.
pass_a: So also, if anyone should defend that those alone are elected unto glory whom God foresees adorned with merits or good works unto the end of their life, and that those alone are reprobated or not-elected whom he foresees perseveringly clinging to demerits or evil works, that person places foresight works, according as they were good or evil, as distinguishing conditions, for whose difference different acts of Divine predestination and reprobation befit diverse humans. Likewise, if anyone should teach that God elects those alone whom he foresees will persevere in faith, and passes by and rejects those alone whom he foresees will persevere in unbelief, that person constitutes this faith and unbelief as distinguishing conditions, for whose discrimination distinct acts of predestination and reprobation fall upon distinct persons. Key lemmas: praevisa opera (foresight works); merita / demerita; fides / infidelitas; perseverare.
pass_b: So too if someone maintains that only those are elected to glory whom God foresees clothed with merits or good works to the end of life, and that only those are reprobated or not elected whom he foresees clinging perseveringly to demerits or evil works — then that person makes foresight works, good or evil, into distinguishing conditions, and by their difference different Divine acts of predestination and reprobation are assigned to different people. Likewise if someone teaches that God elects only those he foresees will persevere in faith, and passes by and rejects only those he foresees will persevere in unbelief — then faith and unbelief become the distinguishing conditions by whose discrimination the distinct acts of predestination and reprobation fall on distinct persons.

title: Cap. 1 prol. IV: common vs distinguishing — Davenant denies foresight discriminators
latin: Videtis jam magnum discrimen inter priores illas conditiones subjecti, quas communes appellavimus, & has posteriores, quas distinguentes nuncupamus. Nam natura Rationalis, & Peccato subdititia, praesupponitur in subjecto praedestinato & reprobato, ut in illis nulla ponatur causa, ratio, aut occasio discriminis; sed Bona opera & Mala, Fides & Infidelitas, ita ponuntur praevisae condiciones in hominibus, ut secundum illas procedat ipsum discrimen hominum praedestinatorum aut reprobatorum. Quanquam ergo concedamus priores conditiones praerequisitas, ut subjectum communiter & promiscue possit subjacere Deo praedestinanti & reprobanti, tamen hasce posteriores, quas multi stabilire conantur, prorsus pernegamus praesupponi & praevideri a Deo in homine praedestinando aut reprobando, aut pro earum diversitate praevisa diversos actus praedestinationis atque reprobationis tendere semper in diversas personas.
pass_a: You see already a great discrimination between those prior conditions of the subject, which we have called common, and these later ones, which we name distinguishing. For rational nature, and nature subjected to sin, is presupposed in the predestined and reprobate subject, so that in them no cause, reason, or occasion of discrimination is placed; but good works and evil, faith and unbelief, are so placed as foresight conditions in humans that according to them the very discrimination of predestined or reprobate humans proceeds. Although therefore we concede the prior conditions as prerequisites, so that the subject commonly and promiscuously can lie under God predestining and reprobating, yet these later ones, which many strive to establish, we utterly deny to be presupposed and foreseen by God in the human to be predestined or reprobated, or that for their foresight diversity diverse acts of predestination and reprobation always tend unto diverse persons. Key lemmas: communes / distinguentes; discrimen; praesupponi; praevideri.
pass_b: You already see the great difference between those earlier subject-conditions we called common, and these later ones we call distinguishing. Rational nature, and nature under sin, is presupposed in the predestined and the reprobate so that nothing in them is set as cause, reason, or occasion of the divide. Good and evil works, faith and unbelief, are instead set as foresight conditions in people so that the very divide between the predestined and the reprobate proceeds according to them. We grant the earlier conditions as prerequisites — so that a subject can, commonly and without distinction, lie under God as he predestines and reprobates. But these later ones, which many try to fix in place, we flatly deny: they are not presupposed or foreseen by God in the person to be predestined or reprobated, nor do different foresight varieties of them always drive different acts of predestination and reprobation onto different persons.

title: Cap. 1 prol. IV: Pontificii admit causes; Arminians mode-without-cause tergiversation
latin: Hisce adhuc praeludam: Pontificios scriptores, qui contendunt bona opera aut peccata praevisa esse conditiones, quas Deus intueatur in praedestinatione ad gloriam & reprobatione, ingenue etiam largiuntur esse causas cur alii eligantur ad gloriam, alii non eligantur; sicuti causae sunt, cum ad executionem decreti ventum fuerit, cur alii admittantur in regnum gloriae, alii excludantur. Sed nuperi Doctores e Schola Arminiana, qui urgent nullam esse electionem aut reprobationem hominum nisi secundum discrimen praevisae in illis fidei aut infidelitatis, negant tamen obstinate fidem esse causam electionis. Dicunt esse Modum secundum quem Deus spectat hominem eligendum, esse antecedens electionis; sed negant esse causam electionis, & simul negant esse effectum, ab electione manentem. Sed hac tergiversatione produnt infirmitatem causae suae. Nam si ponerent fidem solummodo conditionem antecedentem, sine qua non fieret electio hujus aut illius singularis personae, possent probabiliter affirmare se non statuere fidem hujus electionis causam: sed cum insuper doceant, ad positionem fidei poni electionem, ad negationem fidei praevisae negari electionem, aperte tribuunt fidei non nudam antecessionem, sed etiam causalitatem.
pass_a: With these I will still prelude: Pontifical writers, who contend that foresight good works or sins are conditions which God looks upon in predestination unto glory and in reprobation, candidly also grant that they are causes why some are elected unto glory, others not elected; just as they are causes, when it has come to the execution of the decree, why some are admitted into the kingdom of glory, others are excluded. But recent Doctors from the Arminian School, who urge that there is no election or reprobation of humans except according to the discrimination of foresight faith or unbelief in them, yet obstinately deny that faith is the cause of election. They say it is a Mode according to which God regards the human to be elected, that it is an antecedent of election; but they deny that it is the cause of election, and at the same time deny that it is an effect flowing from election. But by this tergiversation they betray the weakness of their cause. For if they were to set faith merely as an antecedent condition without which the election of this or that singular person would not come about, they could probably affirm that they do not establish faith as the cause of this election: but when they further teach that at the positing of faith election is posited, and at the negation of foresight faith election is denied, they openly attribute to faith not bare precedence, but also causality. Key lemmas: Pontificii; Schola Arminiana; modus; causa; antecessio; causalitas; tergiversatio.
pass_b: One more prelude. Pontifical writers who hold that foresight works or sins are conditions God looks to in predestination to glory and in reprobation also frankly grant that those conditions are causes why some are elected to glory and others are not — just as, once the decree is executed, they are causes why some are admitted to the kingdom of glory and others shut out. Recent doctors of the Arminian school press hard that there is no election or reprobation of humans except by the foresight divide of faith or unbelief in them, yet they stubbornly deny that faith is the cause of election. They call it a Mode by which God regards the person to be elected, an antecedent of election; but they deny it is election's cause, and at the same time deny it is an effect flowing from election. That dodge shows how weak their case is. If they set faith only as an antecedent condition without which this or that person's election would not occur, they could fairly say they do not make faith the cause of that election. But when they further teach that faith posited means election posited, and foresight faith denied means election denied, they openly give faith not bare precedence but causality as well.

title: Cap. 1 prol. IV: Fathers treat such conditions as meritorious causes — Aug. Ep. 105
latin: Ausim affirmare Augustinum reliquosque Patres, quandocunque qualitas aut actio aliqua humana ita praerequiritur, ut illa posita ponatur simul consequens aliquod Dei beneficium, illa absente negetur, habere talem qualitatem aut actum causae loco, causae (ut illi loquuntur) suo modo meritoriae. Conditio enim secundum ordinationem Dei postulata, & per gratiam Dei ab homine praestita, habet apud Patres vim & naturam causae meritoriae motivae, quoad beneficium sub tali conditione conferendum. Sic loquitur Augustinus Epist. 105. ubi dicit, ipsam remissionem peccatorum non esse sine aliquo merito, si fides hanc impetrat. Pari ratione electio ad gloriam non erit sine aliquo merito ex parte electi, si fides illam impetrat. Nam meritum apud Patres nihil aliud est, quam opus ex Dei ordinatione alicujus beneficii impetratorium. Si ergo ex praeviso nostro actu credendi conferatur in nos beneficium electionis, non est conditio sine qua non, sed est causa, imo meritum sequentis beneficii, eo sensu quo Patres usurpant hoc meriti vocabulum.
pass_a: I would dare to affirm that Augustine and the remaining Fathers, whenever some human quality or action is so prerequired that when it is posited some consequent benefit of God is posited together with it, and when it is absent that benefit is denied, hold such a quality or act in the place of a cause — of a cause (as they speak) meritorious in its own way. For a condition demanded according to God's ordination, and performed by the human through God's grace, has among the Fathers the force and nature of a meritorious motive cause as to the benefit to be conferred under such a condition. So speaks Augustine in Epistle 105, where he says that the very remission of sins is not without some merit, if faith obtains this. By equal reason election unto glory will not be without some merit on the elect's part, if faith obtains it. For merit among the Fathers is nothing other than a work, by God's ordination, that obtains some benefit. If therefore from our foresight act of believing the benefit of election is conferred upon us, it is not a condition sine qua non, but is a cause — indeed the merit of the following benefit — in that sense in which the Fathers use this word merit. Key lemmas: causa meritoria; meritum; conditio sine qua non; Epist. 105; impetratorium.
pass_b: I dare say Augustine and the other Fathers treat it this way: whenever some human quality or act is so required beforehand that when it is present some following gift of God is present with it, and when it is absent that gift is denied, they set that quality or act in the place of a cause — a cause, as they put it, meritorious in its own way. A condition demanded by God's ordination and performed by the person through God's grace has, for the Fathers, the force and nature of a meritorious motive cause with respect to the benefit conferred under that condition. So Augustine in Epistle 105: the very remission of sins is not without some merit, if faith obtains it. By the same reason, election to glory will not be without some merit on the elect person's side, if faith obtains it. For among the Fathers merit is nothing but a work which, by God's ordination, obtains some benefit. So if the benefit of election is conferred on us from our foresight act of believing, that is not a mere condition sine qua non — it is a cause, indeed the merit of the following benefit, in the sense in which the Fathers use the word merit.

title: Cap. 1 prol. IV: against Pelagian merits and scholastic merita congrua
latin: Nam quando contra Pelagianos disputant, gratiam non dari aut negari secundum merita liberi arbitrii, nihil aliud volunt, quam non dari secundum praevisam conditionem boni aut mali usus ejusdem liberi arbitrii. Si enim Pelagiani hoc evicissent, Patres nunquam negassent esse veram causam gratiae collatae. Sic etiam cum Theologi nostri contra Scholasticos nonnullos contendunt, Deum non praedestinare homines ex praevisis meritis congruis, nihil aliud volunt, quam haec quae appellantur merita congrua non esse conditiones antecedentes ac distinguentes, secundum quas eligantur omnes in quibus illae praevisae fuerant, rejiciantur omnes in quibus non fuerant. Nam si tales conditiones esse demonstraverint, rem confectam habent Scholastici, & nos ultro fatebimur esse causas discriminis electorum & reprobatorum, eo sensu quo causae & meriti vocabulum usurpatur.
pass_a: For when they dispute against the Pelagians that grace is not given or denied according to the merits of free choice, they mean nothing other than that it is not given according to a foresight condition of the good or bad use of that same free choice. For if the Pelagians had proven this, the Fathers would never have denied that it is a true cause of conferred grace. So also when our Theologians contend against some Scholastics that God does not predestine humans from foresight congruent merits, they mean nothing other than that these things called congruent merits are not antecedent and distinguishing conditions according to which all in whom those were foresight are elected, and all in whom they were not are rejected. For if they have demonstrated that such are conditions, the Scholastics have the matter finished, and we of our own accord will confess that they are causes of the discrimination of the elect and the reprobate, in that sense in which the vocabulary of cause and merit is used. Key lemmas: Pelagiani; merita congrua; Scholastici; Theologi nostri.
pass_b: When the Fathers argue against the Pelagians that grace is not given or withheld according to free choice's merits, they mean simply this: it is not given according to a foresight condition of free choice's good or bad use. Had the Pelagians proved that, the Fathers would never have denied it was a true cause of the grace conferred. So too when our theologians contend against some Scholastics that God does not predestine people from foresight congruent merits, they mean that these so-called congruent merits are not antecedent distinguishing conditions by which everyone in whom they were foresight is elected and everyone in whom they were not is rejected. If the Scholastics ever prove such conditions, their case is finished — and we will freely admit that those conditions are causes of the divide between elect and reprobate, in the sense in which cause and merit are spoken of.

title: Cap. 1 prol. IV close: word-tricks on faith; preface ends — theses next
latin: Sunt ergo merae verborum praestigiae, cum aiunt praevisam fidem & infidelitatem esse conditiones, non modo quae antecedunt praedestinationem & reprobationem communiter & promiscue consideratam, sed etiam ex quibus oritur ipsa distinctio electorum & reprobatorum, & tamen negant habere aliquam causalitatem. Nam omnes Theologi qui unquam disputarunt de ratione aut causa electionis, praesumunt id vim causae obtinere, qua posita & a Deo praevisa sequitur; qua negata aut non praevisa non sequitur electio. Atque haec ea sunt quae praefationis loco praemittenda putavi. Totam, quae futura est, disputationem nostram deinceps ad certas quasdam theses revocabimus.
pass_a: They are therefore mere prestiges of words, when they say that foresight faith and unbelief are conditions, not only which antecede predestination and reprobation considered commonly and promiscuously, but also from which arises the very distinction of the elect and the reprobate, and yet deny that they have any causality. For all Theologians who have ever disputed concerning the reason or cause of election presume that that obtains the force of a cause which, when posited and foresight by God, election follows; which, when denied or not foresight, election does not follow. And these are the things which I have thought should be prefaced in the place of a preface. The whole of our forthcoming disputation we will thereafter recall unto certain definite theses. Key lemmas: praestigiae verborum; causalitas; praefatio; theses.
pass_b: So it is mere word-trickery when they say foresight faith and unbelief are conditions — not only ones that precede predestination and reprobation taken commonly and without distinction, but ones from which the very distinction of elect and reprobate arises — and yet deny those conditions any causality. Every theologian who has ever argued the reason or cause of election assumes this: whatever, when posited and foresight by God, brings election with it, and when denied or not foresight leaves election absent, has the force of a cause. These are the points I thought should stand as a preface. From here our whole coming dispute will be drawn into certain fixed theses.
